blindSummary: Trans visitors face serious risk here. The penal code does not explicitly criminalise same-sex conduct, but vague "good morals" provisions make homosexuality "de facto illegal" in practice; there is no anti-discrimination law, no legal gender recognition and no community infrastructure; an authoritarian state that hosts military bases of at least two foreign powers but offers no rights space.

Encyclopedia overview: legality of same-sex activity is ambiguous (no law explicitly criminalising it, but 'obscene acts' provisions); limited protection based on sexual orientation; no gender-identity recognition; LGBTQ people face stigmatisation.

A foreign government's 2023 human-rights report on this country: official assessment including the SOGI section - pervasive social and religious intolerance, LGBTIQ persons afraid to assemble or express themselves, no known prosecutions.

A foreign government's 2015 human-rights report on this country: general human-rights assessment (suppression of opposition, harsh prisons, FGM, trafficking) - baseline context with limited LGBT-specific content.

A foreign tribunal's research response (2012): treatment of sexual minorities in this country (2009 to March 2012) - information scarce; societal norms did not allow public discussion of homosexuality; an LGBTQ travel-news archive reports gay people 'living undercover and in fear' with 'virtually zero tolerance'; but no known reports of societal violence or discrimination; legislation ambiguous (some sources say illegal, one international LGBTI body says not criminalised).
